entries.test: Public employment records and company reporting showing whether workers displaced by LLMs are hired back after those systems fail would test the claim.
entries.note: No deadline is stated; the prediction depends on LLM failure.
The claim assigns an exclusive motive to the scare tactics. Evidence of financial benefits would not establish that exclusive intention.

entries.test: Research and documented company practices available by publication would show whether the entry-level employment changes described in Roose's article had independent evidentiary support.
entries.note: This concerns the evidence available in June 2025.

entries.test: Public audience research, engagement data and studies of editorial coverage would test whether clicks and employment fears drove the narrative's spread.
entries.note: This asserts a causal explanation of audience and media behavior, not merely a private motive.

entries.test: The cited Wall Street Journal article and news archives through June 16, 2025 would establish whether reporting documented companies replacing employees with generative AI.
entries.note: The wording reports what he could find rather than categorically denying that any stories existed. Contrary reporting would challenge its evidentiary implication, without establishing what he personally read.

entries.test: Public workflow comparisons, accuracy evaluations and documented legal incidents would test transcription and translation speed gains, quick-reference utility and associated legal risks.
entries.note: The main assertion is an observed speed improvement; the risk qualification describes a documented capability for harm.

entries.test: Public clinical studies and documented cases would test whether sustained chatbot conversations cause or exacerbate serious psychiatric symptoms.
entries.note: In context, 'driving people insane' has a plain reading as serious psychological harm.
Whether these uses count as transformative is an evaluative judgment without a stated standard.
The assessment turns on 'generic' and 'truly life-changing,' which express judgments of significance.
Beyond the insult, the substantive assertion assigns a purpose to the terminology. Comparing advertised and actual capabilities would not establish that intention.

entries.test: Public evidence available by publication about software engineering duties and verified AI-driven staffing reductions would test whether coding automation replaced engineers rather than merely coinciding with outsourcing.
entries.note: The possible future effect is hedged; the central claim concerns present capabilities and the absence of proof.

entries.test: A public corpus of AI marketing and media coverage through publication would show whether journalists adopted these terms and used 'agent' indiscriminately for LLM activity.
entries.note: Terminology and usage are publicly assessable. The additional assertion about journalists' understanding is less directly observable.
The central assertion concerns an intention to inflate perceived capabilities. Public use of the terms alone cannot settle that motive.
Neither the relevant problems nor the editorial message is specified enough for a shared test of their obviousness or compatibility.
This evaluates the significance of a stock's success and the defensibility of his reasoning. It supplies no common standard for either assessment.

entries.test: Public publisher referral data and studies comparing search traffic with and without Google's AI summaries would establish whether the summaries caused substantial traffic losses by publication.
entries.note: The proposition faithfully isolates the Google traffic claim from the paragraph's other assertions.
